title: Symmetries
goal: Spot mirror symmetry (even), half-turn symmetry (odd), and repeating waves (periodicity) so you only have to sketch half a graph.

beforeThis.skill: Quick check: plug $-x$ into the formula. If the minus signs disappear ($f(-x) = f(x)$), it is even; if one minus sign pops out in front ($f(-x) = -f(x)$), it is odd.

questions.asking: Draw the left half ($x < 0$) of the curve so that the completed graph is symmetric across the $y$-axis.
questions.statement: Suppose $f(x)$ is an even function defined for all real numbers. Below is the curve $y = f(x)$ when $x > 0$. Complete the sketch of the curve.

questions.asking: Draw the left half ($x < 0$) of the curve so that the completed graph has $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry about the origin.
questions.statement: Suppose $f(x)$ is an odd function defined for all real numbers. Below is the curve $y = f(x)$ when $x > 0$. Complete the sketch of the curve.

figures.alt: Coordinate axes showing the same x > 0 curve starting at (0, 0), dipping to a minimum in the fourth quadrant, and rising into the first quadrant.

questions.asking: Plug $-x$ in place of $x$ everywhere in the formula and simplify to show that all the minus signs disappear ($f(-x) = f(x)$).
Find a nonzero constant period $p$ and verify algebraically that $f(x + p) = f(x)$ for all $x$.
Replace $x$ with $-x$ and simplify—remember that $(-x)^4 = x^4$, $(-x)^2 = x^2$, and $\cos(-u) = \cos(u)$!
questions.statement:
$$f(x) = x^4 + 5x^2 + \cos(x^3)$$

What symmetries (even, odd, periodic) does $f(x)$ have?

questions.asking: Plug in $-x$ to see that $x^5$ flips sign while $5x^4$ keeps its sign, so $f(-x)$ matches neither $f(x)$ nor $-f(x)$.
questions.statement:
$$f(x) = x^5 + 5x^4$$

What symmetries (even, odd, periodic) does $f(x)$ have?

questions.asking: Since the basic $\tan u$ function repeats every $\pi$ units, set $\pi p = \pi$ to find the period $p$.
Find the period of $\tan(3x)$ (which is $\pi/3$) and the period of $\sin(4x)$ (which is $2\pi/4 = \pi/2$), then find the smallest positive number that is a whole-number multiple of both.
